title: Factor Immobility and Regional Impacts of Trade Liberalization: Evidence on Poverty from India
research_question: How does exposure to trade liberalization affect poverty and consumption growth across regions within a developing country, and through what mechanisms—such as factor mobility across geographic regions and production sectors, and the role of labor market institutions—do these effects operate across the income distribution?
data_description: The analysis combines several Indian data sources at the district (rural) and NSS region (urban) level. Household consumption, occupation, and industrial affiliation come from the 'thick' rounds of the National Sample Survey (NSS) for 1983, 1987-88, 1993-94, and 1999-2000, covering roughly 75,000 rural and 45,000 urban households per round across about 450 districts and 77 regions in 16 major states. Poverty headcount, poverty depth, average per capita consumption, and consumption percentiles are constructed using Deaton-adjusted poverty lines. The 1991 Indian Census provides three-digit NIC employment shares by district. Tariff data are hand-collected at the six-digit HS level (~5,000 product lines) from Ministry of Finance publications, matched to NIC codes. Nontariff barrier data come from Aksoy (1992) and post-1997 product-level sources. The Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) provides state-industry production and employment data for 1982-1997. Agricultural wages come from the Evenson-McKinsey dataset. The main analysis covers 1987-1997.
institutional_context: In 1991, India undertook a sudden, sweeping trade reform under an IMF Stand-By Arrangement triggered by a balance-of-payments crisis following the first Gulf War. The reforms were externally imposed, rapidly implemented as 'shock therapy', and not preceded by domestic political debate, mitigating typical endogeneity concerns. Average nominal tariffs fell from about 80 percent in 1990 to 37 percent by 1996, the standard deviation of tariffs halved, and the share of products under quantitative restrictions dropped from 87 to 45 percent between 1987 and 1994. Tariff harmonization meant cuts were roughly proportional to initial levels across manufacturing and most agricultural goods, though cereals and oilseeds remained canalized. India's 450 districts had highly varied pre-reform industrial composition, generating differential local exposure. State-level labor regulations, codified through amendments to the 1947 Industrial Disputes Act, varied substantially in flexibility, plausibly shaping cross-sector reallocation.
